title: Kerckhoffs's Principle (1883): Why Secrets Should Live in Keys, Not Code
explainer: In 1883, Dutch cryptographer Auguste Kerckhoffs published six design rules for military ciphers in 'La Cryptographie Militaire'; the most enduring, now called Kerckhoffs's principle, holds that a cryptosystem should stay secure even if everything about it except the key becomes known to an adversary. This is precisely the design logic behind modern secrets management: application code and infrastructure configuration can be widely readable, even public, as long as the actual secrets - API keys, passwords, tokens - are the one thing kept confidential and rotated. Treating 'the system itself' as the secret, instead of just the key, is the mistake Kerckhoffs was already warning against in the 19th century.
